Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

vignette:
Marcus is a 25-year-old salesperson who lives with his girlfriend in a mid-sized American city. He grew up in a European immigrant family and still carries the quiet, self-reliant ethos his father instilled in him. Two years ago, Marcus was working as a civilian contractor in a conflict zone overseas, tasked with logistics support at a small supply depot. One afternoon, a mortar attack struck the compound. He was pinned behind a concrete barrier for nearly an hour while shells landed nearby, one hitting a storage unit less than fifty feet away. He remembers the pressure wave, the ringing in his ears, and the sight of a colleague's blood on the ground. He was not physically injured, but something in him shifted that day.

In the weeks after returning home, Marcus found himself unable to shake a pervasive sense of dread. He began to feel strong negative emotions-fear, anger, and a gnawing guilt that he had not done more to help-that seemed to surface without warning. At work, he struggled to concentrate during sales calls, his mind drifting back to the depot, and he noticed he was snapping at customers over minor frustrations. His girlfriend, Jenna, asked what was wrong, but he could not explain it in a way that made sense. He started avoiding news reports about the region, and he stopped going to bars or crowded restaurants because the noise made his chest tighten.

What frightened Marcus most, however, was the change in how he experienced nighttime. He had come to believe that darkness itself was dangerous-that the quiet hours after midnight were when threats crept closest. He began sleeping with a lamp on, and when Jenna turned it off, he would lie awake, scanning the bedroom shadows for movement. This night vigilance became a nightly ritual: checking the locks three times, pulling the curtains tight, and keeping a flashlight on the nightstand. His concentration worsened during the day because he was exhausted, and the cycle fed itself-the more tired he felt, the more vulnerable he became to the fear that something bad was about to happen.

The emotional toll bled into his relationship. Jenna grew frustrated with his irritability and his refusal to go out after dark. Marcus, in turn, felt ashamed of his own fear, which only deepened his guilt. He began to avoid evening shifts at work, claiming he had appointments, and he lost a commission because he could not focus during a late-afternoon client meeting. He had always been a reliable partner and a steady earner, but now he felt like a stranger in his own life.

It was Jenna who finally insisted he see a therapist. Marcus came to the intake session with his hands clasped tightly in his lap. He said he wanted to stop feeling afraid all the time, but he also confessed that he was terrified of what it meant that he could not feel safe in his own home. He wanted to sleep beside his girlfriend without a light on, and he wanted to stop replaying the sound of that mortar round in his head. But underneath that hope was a deeper fear: that the part of him that had been broken in that depot could never be fixed, and that he would spend the rest of his life checking the locks and waiting for the next explosion.
